content: The Joint Meeting on Pesticide Residues (JMPR) evaluated pyriproxyfen and determined that it is not genotoxic and does not pose a carcinogenic risk to humans. Studies indicate that young animals are not significantly more sensitive to pyriproxyfen than adults. A no-observed-adverse-effect level (NOAEL) of 10 mg/kg body weight per day was established, based on findings of increased relative liver weight and elevated total plasma cholesterol levels in male dogs during two one-year toxicity studies. Using a safety factor of 100, the acceptable daily intake (ADI) was set at 0.1 mg/kg body weight. It was deemed unnecessary to establish a formal guideline value for pyriproxyfen used in vector control in drinking water. A concentration of 0.01 mg/L in drinking water would account for less than 1% of the upper limit of the ADI for a 60 kg adult consuming 2 liters of water daily. Spinosad, a natural product derived from the bacterium Saccharopolyspora spinosa, is a mixture of spinosyn A and spinosyn D. It is used for mosquito control in potable water containers and is specified by the World Health Organization (WHO) under the WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme (WHOPES) for use against Aedes aegypti. The recommended application dose is 5 mg/L, with an expected efficacy duration of 4–6 weeks under field conditions. WHO has evaluated three formulations of spinosad for mosquito larviciding: granules (636/GR), aqueous suspension concentrate (636/SC), and tablets for direct application (636/DT). In a 14-day study, a single tablet added to a 200-liter water container resulted in a maximum concentration of approximately 52 µg/L. No acute reference dose was set due to spinosad's low acute toxicity. Temephos, an organophosphorus insecticide, is primarily used as a larvicide to control mosquitoes in ponds, marshes, and potable water containers. It is approved by WHO under WHOPES for vector control in drinking water sources, with a recommended dosage not exceeding 1 mg/L. The NOAEL for temephos was determined to be 3 mg/kg body weight per day, based on inhibition of brain acetylcholinesterase activity in rats. Using a safety factor of 100, an ADI of 0.023 mg/kg body weight was calculated. Due to its low solubility and high octanol-water partition coefficient, temephos is unlikely to remain in solution at the maximum recommended dose, and slow-release formulations are expected to result in much lower concentrations than the approved dose of 1 mg/L. The WHO Guidelines for Drinking-Water Quality provide comprehensive recommendations for ensuring safe drinking water. These guidelines are supported by various documents that offer detailed information on water safety planning, microbial and chemical risk assessment, and management strategies. Examples include guidance on managing risks from cyanobacteria, microplastics, pharmaceuticals, and radionuclides in drinking water, as well as practical tools for implementing water safety plans in small communities. Additionally, WHO publications address specific topics such as the health significance of calcium and magnesium in drinking water, the safety of desalinated water, and the prevention of waterborne diseases like legionellosis. These resources aim to assist policymakers, water suppliers, and public health professionals in improving water quality and ensuring public health protection.
